title: Why Parties Write Governing Plans Before They Win
hook: Long before an election, the out-of-power side is often already drafting exactly what it would do if it won — a governing blueprint built to be ready on day one.
key_points: Parties and allied think tanks often draft detailed policy blueprints while out of power, rather than waiting until after an election to plan.
The best-known recent example is the Heritage Foundation's 'Project 2025,' a blueprint for a future Republican administration.
In 2026, Democratic-aligned groups built their own version, nicknamed 'Project 2029,' with policy proposals ready for a future administration to adopt quickly.
One proposal targets everyday frustrations — robocalls, long hold times, hidden fees — sometimes called the 'annoyance economy.'
These blueprints function as a dry run: they let a party debate and refine its agenda before it has to govern, so it can move fast if it wins.
content_html: Writing a governing plan usually sounds like something that happens after you win. In practice, the more common pattern is the opposite: parties and the think tanks around them often draft detailed blueprints for what they'd do in office long before any votes are counted.
extra_html: The best-known recent version is the Heritage Foundation's "Project 2025," built for a future Republican administration. NPR's Greg Rosalsky reports that Democratic-aligned groups have now built their own answer, nicknamed "Project 2029" — including proposals aimed at everyday frustrations sometimes grouped under the "annoyance economy," like robocalls, long hold times, and hidden fees. Whatever their politics, these documents serve the same structural purpose: they let a party fight over and settle its agenda while it's still out of power, so there's a ready-made plan to execute the moment it wins — rather than trying to figure out what to do only after taking office. (This card describes a general practice used across the U.S. political spectrum.)

flashcards.prompt: What is a pre-election policy blueprint, and why do parties or allied groups write them?
flashcards.back_html: A detailed governing plan drafted while a party is out of power, so its agenda is debated and ready to act on quickly if it wins office.

flashcards.prompt: What is 'Project 2029,' as described in NPR's 2026 reporting?

choices.text: A Democratic-aligned policy blueprint modeled on the Heritage Foundation's 'Project 2025'
An official piece of legislation already passed by Congress
A government agency created to reduce consumer complaints

flashcards.explanation_html: It's a blueprint built by outside allies, not a law — the same kind of preparatory document Project 2025 was for the other party.

flashcards.prompt: Why do policy blueprints like this get built well before an election?

choices.text: To let a party debate and refine its agenda in advance, so it can move quickly if it takes power
Because federal law requires every party to publish a governing plan two years ahead
Because think tanks are barred from writing policy after an election

flashcards.explanation_html: There's no legal requirement — it's a strategic choice to be ready to govern immediately rather than start planning after winning.
